questions.q: Why use alias() on an aggregated column like avg("fare_amount")?
options: alias() is required syntax or the aggregation will fail
It only matters when grouping by more than one column
Without it, Spark names the column something like avg(fare_amount), which is awkward to reference in later steps
It converts the column to a string type
questions.explain: alias() gives the computed column a clean, readable name like avg_fare instead of the default expression-based name.

questions.q: What does grouping by both VendorID and passenger_count produce?
options: One row total, combining both columns into a single aggregate
An error, since PySpark only supports grouping by one column
The same result as grouping by VendorID alone
One row per unique combination of VendorID and passenger_count
questions.explain: Grouping by multiple columns works the same way as pandas: each unique combination becomes its own group.

questions.q: Why join the trips DataFrame to the taxi zone lookup table?
options: The join is required before Spark can read the Parquet file at all
A raw trip record only has a numeric PULocationID, and the join turns that into a real, readable Zone and Borough name
It removes all rows with a missing fare_amount
It converts the DataFrame into a pandas DataFrame
questions.explain: This mirrors the join pattern from the Data Engineering Foundations course's PySpark chapter, applied to pickup location here.

questions.q: Why use a "left" join when joining trips to the zone lookup table?
options: It removes every trip that doesn't have a valid fare_amount
It only works when both DataFrames have exactly the same number of rows
It keeps every trip record even if its location ID happens to have no matching row in the lookup table
A left join is required syntax and has no real effect on which rows are kept
questions.explain: An inner join would silently drop any trip whose PULocationID doesn't match the lookup table; a left join keeps it with nulls instead.

questions.q: In the fare-by-zone example, why join and filter before grouping, rather than after?
options: It makes no difference to the result in any scenario
Grouping needs the readable zone name and clean fare values already in place to produce a meaningful aggregation by zone
PySpark requires filter() to be the very last step in any chain
Joining after grouping is actually faster in every case
questions.explain: The pipeline joins first to get zone names, filters out bad fares, and only then aggregates by the now-readable zone column.
